summary.text: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles released from the Sun's outermost atmospheric layer, the corona.
This plasma mostly consists of electrons, protons and alpha particles, and it varies in density, temperature and speed over time.
Its particles escape the Sun's gravity because of the corona's heat, and related phenomena include the aurora and comet tails that always point away from the Sun.

facts.label: Speed far out
facts.value: 250-750 km/s, faster than fast magnetosonic waves

facts.label: Slowdown point
facts.value: Flow stops being supersonic at the termination shock

items.prompt: A comet loops around the Sun and heads back out into space. Which way will its tail point?

options.label: Behind the comet, along its path
Toward the Sun, pulled by gravity
Away from the Sun, whichever way the comet travels
Sideways, along the comet's orbit

items.explain: Comet tails always point away from the Sun, regardless of the direction in which the comet is travelling, because the Sun emits a steady stream of particles.

items.prompt: The Sun's gravity is strong, yet a stream of particles still flows away from it. What lets those particles break free?

options.label: Their high energy, from the corona's high temperature
A pull from the planets as they pass
Gravity dropping to zero just above the surface
Their being lighter than any gas on Earth

items.explain: The particles escape the Sun's gravity because of their high energy, a result of the high temperature of the corona.

items.prompt: The corona is so hot that its pressure cannot be held back by gravity alone. What did Parker conclude the gas must do?

options.label: Stay put in a still shell around the Sun
Flow outward, speeding up to supersonic beyond a critical point
Fall back and sink into the Sun
Flow outward at one steady slow speed

items.explain: Parker argued a million-degree corona cannot remain static: pressure forces must drive an expanding flow that goes from subsonic near the Sun to supersonic beyond a critical point.

items.prompt: A scientist in the early 1900s finds the northern lights almost never switch off. What did he conclude about particles from the Sun?

options.label: They arrive only in rare bursts
They arrive only during solar eclipses
They are all positively charged
Earth is being continually bombarded by them

items.explain: Birkeland's surveys showed auroral activity was almost uninterrupted, so he concluded the Earth was continually bombarded by particles from the Sun.

items.prompt: Some early scientists thought the Sun sends out only one kind of electric charge. What did Birkeland propose instead?

options.label: Both negative electrons and positive ions
Only electrons, the lightest particles
Only positive ions
Neutral atoms with no charge

items.explain: Birkeland proposed that the rays from the Sun are neither exclusively negative nor positive but of both kinds.

items.prompt: In 1859 a bright flash on the Sun was followed a day later by a powerful geomagnetic storm. What is the storm now attributed to?

options.label: A comet's tail sweeping past Earth
A sudden dimming of the Sun
A coronal mass ejection arriving near Earth
Earth passing through a sunspot

items.explain: The storm is now attributed to the arrival of the coronal mass ejection in near-Earth space and its interaction with the Earth's magnetosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A wind of particles
paragraphs.text: The solar wind is an outflow of charged particles from the corona, the outermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere. It is a plasma made mostly of electrons, protons and alpha particles, with kinetic energies between 0.5 and 10 keV. Small amounts of heavier nuclei travel with it, including carbon, oxygen, silicon and iron. The interplanetary magnetic field is laid over this flow.

paragraphs.heading: How it escapes the Sun
paragraphs.text: The particles break free of the Sun's gravity because they carry so much energy. That energy comes from the corona's high temperature, which is itself produced by the coronal magnetic field. The border where the corona ends and the wind begins is called the Alfvén surface. Beyond a few solar radii the wind moves at 250–750 km/s, faster than fast magnetosonic waves, which makes it supersonic, and it stays that way until the termination shock. Its density, temperature and speed change over time and across solar latitude and longitude.

paragraphs.heading: Signs we can see
paragraphs.text: The solar wind is tied to the aurora, the northern and southern lights. It is also linked to geomagnetic storms, which can change the direction of magnetic field lines, and to comet tails that always face away from the Sun. In the 1950s Ludwig Biermann noticed that a comet's tail points away from the Sun whatever direction the comet is heading. He proposed that a steady stream of particles from the Sun pushes the tail back.

paragraphs.heading: Early hints
paragraphs.text: In a 1610 letter to Galileo, Johannes Kepler wrote of a "heavenly breeze" that pushes comets out into space. In 1859 Carrington and Richard Hodgson saw what would later be named a solar flare, and a powerful geomagnetic storm came the next day. Carrington suspected the two were connected; today the storm is put down to a coronal mass ejection reaching the space around Earth. Kristian Birkeland's surveys showed auroras going on almost without a break, and he concluded that Earth is constantly hit by particles from the Sun. In 1916 he proposed that these include both negative electrons and positive ions.

paragraphs.heading: Parker names the wind
paragraphs.text: The mathematician Sydney Chapman worked out that the corona carries heat so well that it must stretch beyond Earth's orbit. Biermann went over his results with Eugene Parker at the University of Chicago, and Parker also talked about the corona with Chapman. He argued that a corona at a million degrees cannot stay still: pressure must drive it outward, speeding up from slower than sound near the Sun to faster than sound past a critical point. He picked the name solar wind because the older term suggested single particles shot out, when it is really an ordinary flow of gas. By his own account, the maths took just "four lines of algebra".

paragraphs.heading: A spiral, and a cold welcome
paragraphs.text: Parker's theory also predicted the shape of the Sun's magnetic field in the outer Solar System. As the Sun turns, field lines carried outward get wound into a spiral in the ecliptic, now called the Parker spiral. The idea was not welcomed at first: when Parker sent it to The Astrophysical Journal in 1958, two reviewers advised rejecting it. In 1960 his Chicago colleague Joseph W. Chamberlain offered a slower solution, the "solar breeze", which Marco Velli later showed to be unstable.
